quarterly_data.signal: A RARE DOWNWARD REVISION TO A DATA-CENTER PIPELINE — AND WHY IT MATTERS: Exelon's data-center growth pipeline now shows a combined 36 GIGAWATTS, DOWN ROUGHLY 11 GW FROM THE 43 GW previously cited. CFO Jeanne Jones attributes the cut not to demand weakness but to Exelon's own screening discipline: it developed TRANSMISSION SECURITY AGREEMENTS (TSAs) that 'never existed in our regions', and its cluster process now requires a customer to sign a TSA and, importantly, 'PUT UP COLLATERAL BEHIND THAT'. The result: 'what this update reflects is we have now WEEDED OUT SPECULATIVE PROJECTS, and it gives us proactive insight into what is real.' Exelon says it has deliberately kept capex increases consistent with historical levels and only committed capital that was 'certain and durable', alongside its stance on CO-LOCATION and fair cost allocation to shield existing customers from infrastructure costs. This is a useful reality-check datapoint on how much of the headline AI interconnection queue is firm versus speculative.
quarterly_data.figure: Data-centre pipeline cut 43 GW -> 36 GW after TSA + COLLATERAL requirements weeded out speculative projects

quarterly_data.signal: HYPERSCALER CONTRACTING AND COOLING-ARCHITECTURE MIX: 'many of our hyperscalers now have -- whether it be a MASTER PURCHASE AGREEMENT or a LONG-TERM CAPACITY COMMITMENT with us. So we're gaining a lot of visibility to what they need' (CEO Dave Regnery). On technology mix, Trane sees data-center demand weighted TOWARD AIR-COOLED chillers and, importantly, toward CLOSED-LOOP systems with less evaporative cooling — management pushing back on the 'data centers waste water' narrative. Historical rule of thumb has inverted: water-cooled used to signal a 40-year data center and air-cooled a 20-year one, but that shifted given capacity requirements, and modern air-cooled technology now reaches efficiencies similar to or better than water-cooled. Trane is also 'helping many of our hyperscalers and our big colos design' systems for the DIRECT CURRENT versus alternating current transition.
